quiz.question: How has the global rate of children dying before age five changed since 1990?
options: It has stayed roughly the same
It has fallen by more than half

surveyResult.mostCommonWrongAnswer: It has stayed roughly the same

headline: The Quiet Miracle Almost Nobody Talks About at Dinner Parties
teaser: Something has been happening to children under five -- something so large in scale that it ought to dominate every conversation about human progress. It doesn't. The gap between what has actually occurred and what people believe has occurred is one of the widest in the entire Gapminder dataset. When researchers posed this question to audiences in fourteen countries, the pattern was consistent: people who consider themselves well-informed got it wrong at rates that would embarrass a random number generator. The story involves billions of lives, decades of quiet effort, and a change so undramatic in its daily unfolding that nobody thought to write a headline about it. Until now, perhaps.
metaDescription: In 1990, 12 million children died before their fifth birthday each year. Today that number has more than halved. 68% of people don't know this.
summary: In 1990, roughly 93 out of every 1,000 children born worldwide died before reaching their fifth birthday. By 2024, that figure had dropped to around 36 per 1,000. In absolute terms, annual child deaths fell from approximately 12.6 million to under 5 million — even as the number of births remained broadly stable. This is arguably the most important thing that has happened in the world in the past three decades, and most people have never heard of it.
nuance: The global average masks severe inequality. In sub-Saharan Africa, the under-five mortality rate remains above 70 per 1,000 in several countries, while in Western Europe it sits below 4. The rate of improvement has also slowed since 2015, raising concerns about whether SDG targets for 2030 can be met.
brysonAside: To put the improvement in perspective: the number of children's lives saved each year compared to 1990 rates is roughly equivalent to the entire population of Portugal. Every year. And hardly anyone thought to throw a party.

emailDigestLine: The equivalent of an entire country's population in children's lives saved every year — and it barely made the news.
premiumTeaser: The story of how child mortality fell is, in significant part, the story of a remarkably cheap packet of salt, sugar, and water — and the obstinate Bangladeshi doctor who insisted it could work. There is also the matter of what happened in the countries where it didn't fall, which turns out to be a different kind of instructive.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Have students estimate the 1990 vs 2024 figures before revealing. Connects to SDG 3 (Good Health) and introduces oral rehydration therapy as a case study in cost-effective intervention.
publishingNote: IGME and OWID data closely aligned. Nuance addresses inequity and SDG shortfall honestly.

learn.title: "The Blue Sweater" by Jacqueline Novogratz (summary)
learn.description: Novogratz traces a single blue sweater from her closet in Virginia to a boy in Rwanda, weaving a story about how global health interventions connect lives across continents in ways we rarely see.

fund.description: Gavi is the organisation behind the vaccination campaigns that drove much of this chart's decline. When you see child mortality falling, you are largely looking at Gavi's supply chain at work.

act.action: Check if your workplace pension excludes tobacco stocks
act.description: Tobacco is still a leading contributor to child mortality through secondhand smoke and maternal health effects. Most pension providers now offer tobacco-free options — finding out if yours does takes a single email.
